title: Supreme Court: Grandson Has No Birthright in Property His Father Inherited After Partition
case_name: J. Rajesh (minor, through his mother and natural guardian J. Gomathi) v. M. Kumaran (dead, through LRs)
card_summary: The Supreme Court on 6 November 2026 dismissed a partition suit filed on behalf of a minor grandson, holding that a father's share in property inherited under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act becomes his separate property once partitioned among the Class I heirs. The grandson had no birthright in that share by coparcenary, since succession opened before his birth.
card_tip: A father's inherited and partitioned share is his personal property; children get no automatic birthright in it by birth and must rely on a will or a family settlement instead.
verification_notes: AUDIENCE: HNI (family-owned property and succession). TARGET QUERY: can a grandson claim share in grandfather's property after it was partitioned among his father's generation. DEMAND EVIDENCE: none seen (the ruling was reported the same week by at least seven outlets including wire-service pickups, suggesting reader interest, but no search-volume data was seen). Cross-verified across Verdictum (which gives the full caption and the citation 2026 INSC 1208), LawBeat, Raw Law, ETV Bharat and Outlook Money, which agree that a bench of Justices Augustine George Masih and Sunita Agarwal, on 6 November 2026, dismissed a 1997 partition suit over a Chennai property, holding that once the grandfather's estate devolved on his Class I heirs under Section 8 and was partitioned among them in 1994, each heir's share became that heir's separate property and did not revive as joint family property for the next generation; the appellant, not being a surviving coparcener when the grandfather died and born after succession opened, could not claim a birthright share, and as a male could not invoke the Tamil Nadu Amendment Act, 1989 (Section 29-A), which benefits only daughters. The grandfather's name appears as 'N Ramachandran' in most reports; one report spells it differently, so the first name alone is used in this card's summary where needed and the full case caption is taken from Verdictum. The appeal number given in one source only (Civil Appeal No. 7020 of 2012) was not independently cross-checked and is omitted from the citation field.
